1.note: Amos is speaking to the wealthy women of Samaria, whom he calls **cows of Bashan**, although he knows that they cannot hear him. He is doing this to show his listeners in a strong way how he feels about the way these women oppress the poor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about these women. Alternate translation: [Hear this word about the cows of Bashan]

Amos is speaking of the wealthy women of Samaria as if they were **cows of Bashan**, that is, well-fed cattle grazing in rich pasture on the hillsides overlooking Samaria. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you well-fed, pampered women]

Amos is speaking of the cruel way that these wealthy women are mistreating the needy people as if they were cattle **crushing** them underfoot. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the ones mistreating the needy]

Amos is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

Amos is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [people who are needy]

The implication is that the **masters** of these women are their husbands whom they should be serving. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the ones saying to their husbands]
If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this as an indirect quotation. Alternate translation: [to their masters that they should bring them something to drink]

The women are leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Bring drinks to us]

2.note: Following the custom of the culture, the Lord Yahweh is swearing an oath and guaranteeing it by something sacred, his own **holiness**. Use a natural way in your language to express an oath. Alternate translation: [The Lord Yahweh has solemnly promised, as surely as he is holy]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **holiness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [by his holy name]

Amos did not always say who was speaking or who was being addressed. Here, it seems to be the beginning of what Yahweh said but the ULT shows it as Amos telling us what Yahweh said (no quote marks). If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark this as a direct quote of Yahweh as in the UST.

Yahweh is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and you should take notice that the days]
The pronoun **he** refers to their enemies and **you** to the women of Samaria. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [when your enemies will lift you women up]

2.q: וְ⁠נִשָּׂ֤א אֶתְ⁠כֶם֙ בְּ⁠צִנּ֔וֹת וְ⁠אַחֲרִיתְ⁠כֶ֖ן בְּ⁠סִיר֥וֹת דּוּגָֽה
2.note: Amos is speaking of the women being carried away as captives as if they were fish that someone catches **with hooks** or **hooks of fishery.** If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when he will carry you away as captives, every last one of you, as easily as a fisherman uses hooks to catch fish]

3.note: Amos is using the phrase **a woman** as a common expression of the culture to mean “each woman.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [each woman]

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [going out through the break in the wall that is in front of her]
Amos is interjecting the phrase **the declaration of Yahweh** to indicate that what is being said comes with Yahweh’s authority.

The word translated as **toward Harmon** could be: (1) the name of a place that is now unknown. (2) a word that means “rule”or “dominion.” Alternate translation: [and you will cast away dominion] or [and you will let go of your rule]

4.q: בֹּ֤אוּ בֵֽית־אֵל֙ וּ⁠פִשְׁע֔וּ הַ⁠גִּלְגָּ֖ל הַרְבּ֣וּ לִ⁠פְשֹׁ֑עַ
4.note: Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here and throughout the next verse. He is telling them that they are doing these rituals with the wrong motives and thus sinning. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You should not go to Bethel and sin there, nor to Gilgal and sin even more]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **transgress**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and go against Yahweh’s commands]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and bring your tithes every three days]

5.q: וְ⁠קַטֵּ֤ר מֵֽ⁠חָמֵץ֙ תּוֹדָ֔ה וְ⁠קִרְא֥וּ נְדָב֖וֹת הַשְׁמִ֑יעוּ
5.note: Yahweh actually means to communicate the opposite of the literal meaning of what he is saying here. If a speaker of your language would not do that, you could translate the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I take no pleasure when you make a thank offering from what is leavened, and loudly announce your freewill offerings]

Amos assumes that readers will know that Yahweh had forbidden any burning of bread that contains yeast as a sacrifice to him (Leviticus 2:11). You could include this information in a footnote if that would be helpful to your readers.

The phrase **call out freewill offerings** could mean: (1) that people were to publicly announce when they brought a gift to Yahweh. This would be against the purpose of these offerings which were to be given whenever someone wanted to give something to Yahweh, Alternate translation: [and announce that you are bringing a freewill offering] or (2) that people would be required to bring freewill offerings. This would be the opposite of the meaning of freewill offerings, but perhaps what the people were doing. Alternate translation: [and announce that I require freewill offerings]

If it would be more natural in your language, you could move this phrase to the beginning of verse 4, since **For thus you have loved** gives the reason for these instructions that Yahweh is giving the people that are contradictory to what he has actually commanded them to do. Alternate translation: [Since you so love to do these things, sons of Israel, go ahead to Bethel]
Amos is speaking as if the Israelites were actually the **sons** of the patriarch **Israel**, who was also known as Jacob. Alternate translation: [you people of Israel]
See how you translated the very similar phrase “the declaration of Yahweh” in verse 3.

6.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I gave** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who sent the famine. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And even I myself gave to you]

Yahweh is using **cleanness of teeth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “famine,” since people who have nothing to eat do not dirty their teeth. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I caused you to have famine]

6.q: נִקְי֤וֹן שִׁנַּ֨יִם֙ בְּ⁠כָל־עָ֣רֵי⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠חֹ֣סֶר לֶ֔חֶם בְּ⁠כֹ֖ל מְקוֹמֹֽתֵי⁠כֶ֑ם
6.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way as in the UST. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [cleanness of teeth in all your cities, indeed I gave to you lack of bread in all your places]
Yahweh is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and lack of any food]

Yahweh is speaking of the people repenting and giving him their loyalty again as if they would **return** to him along a road they were traveling on. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [yet you did not repent and give me your full allegiance]

Yahweh uses the word **yet** here to indicate a contrast between the famine that he sent and the response that he expected from the people. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but in spite of that, you did not return]
See how you translated the same phrase in verse 3.

7.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I** separately, even though the verb translated as **I withheld** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he himself is the one who sent the drought. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [And also I myself withheld from you]

7.q: וְ⁠הִמְטַרְתִּי֙ עַל־עִ֣יר אֶחָ֔ת וְ⁠עַל־עִ֥יר אַחַ֖ת לֹ֣א אַמְטִ֑יר חֶלְקָ֤ה אַחַת֙ תִּמָּטֵ֔ר וְ⁠חֶלְקָ֛ה
7.note: Yahweh uses the word **and** here to indicate a contrast between the city on which he made it rain and the city on which he did not make it rain. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And I made it rain on one city, but on another city I did not make it rain; one portion was rained on, but another portion]

The expression **was rained on** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [I sent rain on one portion]

It might seem that the expression **a portion which it did not rain on it** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [and another portion that received no rain]

8.note: Yahweh is using **two–three cities** as a common expression of the culture to mean a small but indefinite number of cities. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And a few cities staggered]

Here, **cities** represents the people living in the cities that were suffering from lack of water. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the people from a few cities]
See how you translated this in 4:6.
See how you translated the same phrase in verse 3.

9.note: Yahweh is speaking of afflicting their crops with blight and mildew as if he had physically **struck** them with a blow. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I afflicted your crops with blight and mildew]
See how you translated this in 4:6.
See how you translated the same phrase in verse 3.

10.note: Yahweh is using **a plague in the way of Egypt** to mean a plague like the ones that he sent on the Egyptians. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [a plague like the ones I sent on the Egyptians]

Here, **the sword** represents “warfare.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I allowed your enemies to kill your young men in warfare]

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. He means that Yahweh caused the stench of the corpses of those killed to rise from where the Israelites were camped. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [the stench of the corpses in your camp]
See how you translated this in 4:6.
See how you translated the same phrase in verse 3.

11.q: הָפַ֣כְתִּי בָ⁠כֶ֗ם כְּ⁠מַהְפֵּכַ֤ת אֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־סְדֹ֣ם וְ⁠אֶת־עֲמֹרָ֔ה
11.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah** so completely that nothing was left of them, so the destruction that Yahweh brought on the Israelites was devastating. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I brought devastating destruction among you, just as God so completely destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah that nothing was left of them]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a firebrand snatched from a burning** is charred and barely saved, so the Israelites who survived were rescued only barely and at great cost. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and some of you barely survived, as though you had been pulled out of a fire at the last moment]

The expression **snatched from a burning** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [like a firebrand that someone snatched]
See how you translated this in 4:6.
See how you translated the same phrase in verse 3.

12.note: The word translated as **Therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you would not return to me, this is what I will do to you, Israel]
**Israel** represents the people of Israel. Alternate translation: [to you Israelites]

12.q: עֵ֚קֶב כִּֽי־זֹ֣את אֶֽעֱשֶׂה־לָּ֔⁠ךְ הִכּ֥וֹן לִ⁠קְרַאת־אֱלֹהֶ֖י⁠ךָ יִשְׂרָאֵֽל
12.note: The words translated as **for the reason that** indicate that what follows is a reason for the command that comes after it. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason. Alternate translation: [and since I will do this to you, prepare to meet your God, Israel]

The word translated as **prepare** is an imperative, but it communicates a solemn warning rather than a command. Use a form in your language that communicates a warning. Alternate translation: [be prepared to meet your God]

13.note: The word translated as **For** connects this description of Yahweh to what he has just said, that they should “prepare to meet” their God, and the word **behold** calls attention to what follows. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [In fact, you will need to prepare to meet your God by carefully considering that he is]

This could mean: (1) God declares to people their own inward thoughts and motivations, as in the UST. (2) God reveals to people what he, God, is thinking. Alternate translation: [and declaring to man God’s own plans]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thought**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he is thinking]

This could mean: (1) God makes everything from morning light to the darkness of night. Alternate translation: [making all times of light and darkness] or (2) God causes morning to become night. Alternate translation: [making dawn into darkness]

Amos is speaking of Yahweh ruling over the whole earth as if he were **treading on the high places of the earth**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and ruling over the whole earth]

Amos is using this possessive form to mean the God who commands the armies of heaven. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who commands the armies of heaven]
Amos is using the term **name** to represent who Yahweh is or to refer to the Yahweh’s reputation. Alternate translation: [this is who he is]
